extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception (Alice/Mayo Step 2B), including when elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, mere instructions to apply an exception, or meaningful limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a determination whether the additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration overlaps with other Step 2B considerations (improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity). Key points: (1) An additional element known in the art can still be unconventional or non-routine — novelty/obviousness is separate from eligibility (e.g., Enfish). (2) A prior art search should not be necessary; examiners should rely on what courts or those of ordinary skill recognize as widely prevalent or in common use — conclude conventionality only when examiner can readily conclude that the element is widely prevalent or in common use (example: glucose-sensing earring contrasted with routinely-used glucose monitoring). (3) Even if individual elements are conventional, their combination may amount to an inventive concept (Diamond v. Diehr; Rapid Litig. Mgmt.; BASCOM). The specification may indicate additional elements are well-known or conventional; courts sometimes treat conventionality as appropriate for judicial notice. A rejection should only be made if an examiner, relying on expertise in the art, can readily conclude the additional elements do not amount to significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for formulating such rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized examples of well-understood, routine, conventional computer functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts have recognized certain computer functions as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner (e.g., at a high level of generality) or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples the courts have recognized include: (i) receiving or transmitting data over a network (using the Internet to gather data; forwarding information); (ii) performing repetitive calculations (recomputing or readjusting values); (iii) electronic recordkeeping (creating/maintaining shadow accounts, updating activity logs); (iv) storing and retrieving information in memory; (v) electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (OCR); (vi) a web browser's back and forward button functionality. The listing is not exhaustive and does not imply all computer functions are conventional (see decisions like DDR Holdings, Amdocs, BASCOM for eligible computer-implemented claims). Courts have found claims ineligible where the claim as a whole amounts to generic computer functions used to implement an abstract idea; conversely, combinations that perform non-generic functions may be significantly more (DDR Holdings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized examples of well-understood, routine, conventional laboratory techniques (life sciences)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the life science arts, certain laboratory techniques have been recognized by courts as well-understood, routine, conventional activity when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (i) determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means; (ii) using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA; (iii) detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample; (iv) immunizing a patient against a disease; (v) analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants; (vi) freezing and thawing cells; (vii) amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences; (viii) hybridizing a gene probe. These techniques, when recited generically, have been treated as conventional in decisions such as Mayo, Ariosa/Sequenom, Rapid Litig. Mgmt., Ambry Genetics, and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other activities courts have found well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have recognized various non-technical or business/clerical activities as well-understood, routine, conventional when claimed in a merely generic manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: recording a customer's order; shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards; restricting public access to media by requiring a consumer to view an advertisement; identifying undeliverable mail items and decoding data on them; presenting offers and gathering statistics; determining an estimated outcome and setting a price; arranging a hierarchy of groups, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information, and determining the price. Examiners should treat such generic recitations cautiously, analyzing them with other Step 2B considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful limitations (Other Meaningful Limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim directed to a judicial exception to be patent-eligible, it must include additional features that ensure the claim applies the exception in a meaningful way — i.e., add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the exception to a particular technological environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'meaningful limitations' describes additional elements that provide an inventive concept; considerations in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(d) are examples of meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr — steps applying a mathematical equation in a specific automated rubber-molding process were meaningful because they limited practical application; Classen — immunization step integrated analytical results into a specific tangible method. The claim should add limitations beyond mere implementation on a generic computer or mere linkage to a technological environment. Examiners must consider additional elements both individually and in combination; when appropriate, examiners may explain on the record why the additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim's additional elements may be nothing more than mere instructions to apply a judicial exception (e.g., an abstract idea or law of nature); such recitations do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The additional element(s) must do 'more than simply state the [judicial exception] while adding the words 'apply it'' (Alice/Mayo). Examples: Mayo — measuring metabolites was mere instruction to apply the law; Alice — recitation of a computer to perform intermediated settlement was mere implementation on a generic computer; Benson — BCD-to-binary conversion claim had no substantial practical application except in connection with a computer. Implementing an abstract idea on a generic computer is insufficient. Requiring more than mere instructions does not mean claims must be narrow — both broad eligible and narrow ineligible claims exist; examiners should evaluate each claim on its merits and consider overlap with other Step 2B considerations. For claim limitations that do not amount to more than 'apply it,' examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection (e.g., 'implementing on a generic computer does not add significantly more').

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment whether a claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (result-oriented claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: One key indicator of a mere instruction to apply an exception is whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome, failing to recite details of how the solution is accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-oriented or highly functional claim language that covers any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished is equivalent to saying 'apply it' and typically does not provide significantly more. Courts have found such claims ineligible (Electric Power Group; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network). In contrast, claiming a particular solution or specific way to achieve an outcome may provide significantly more. Example: Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One — claims that were result-oriented and lacked details of how modifications were performed were held ineligible. Examiners should look for concrete, specific steps/mechanisms rather than mere high-level result language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether additional elements meaningfully limit a judicial exception, examiners must consider both the individual additional elements and their combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An additional element may be enough on its own to qualify as 'significantly more' if it meaningfully limits the exception; however, even if individual elements do not, their combination may amount to significantly more (Diamond v. Diehr; BASCOM). Examiners should analyze and explain when the combination produces a non-conventional, non-generic arrangement that provides a technical improvement.
